definition: An operator control that revokes an agent's access so its next call is refused. Here it can be pulled for one agent or for all of them, and it is checked on every call. How a real product implements it is as modelled in the demo environment, UNVERIFIED against product documentation.

Withdraw access that was already granted. In this demo a revoke marks the agent's live tokens as revoked at the stub token service and shuts token issuance for that agent. As modelled in the demo environment, UNVERIFIED against product documentation.

A limit on how many calls an agent may make in a sliding time window. The call at the limit is allowed; the next one inside the window trips the agent. The window and count here are invented demo numbers, not any product default.

A limit on what an agent may spend: a token budget and a money budget from an invented price table. Each admitted call is charged once, a refused call costs nothing, and spending exactly up to the budget is allowed. Prices here are illustrative, not any vendor's.
A rate window that moves with time: a call exactly one window old no longer counts. It avoids the burst that a fixed clock-minute window allows at the boundary.

The automatic stop when a cap is breached. The agent moves from armed to tripped, its tokens are revoked and issuance shuts, with no human involved. Rate trips can auto-reset after a cooldown; cost trips and manual kills do not.

The four states of an agent. Armed means running under its caps. Tripped means a cap stopped it automatically. Killed means an operator stopped it. Reset means it was restored, by an operator unrevoke or by an auto-reset after a cooldown.

A token that expires soon after it is issued. If a gateway only checks a token locally, a short lifetime limits how long a revoked token keeps working. The lifetimes here are invented demo numbers, not a product default.

The time between the revoke and the first refused call. With a check on every call it is as short as the agent's next call. With local token validation and a stale revocation list, calls can still get through until the list refreshes or the token expires. Measured in the stale-token-gap scenario; no real latency is claimed.

A call already admitted when the stop lands. In this demo it is not interrupted by default: it finishes, is flagged completed-after-stop, and stays charged. Cancelling it is an option of the demo, not a documented product behaviour. The next call is refused.
How much else a stop affects. Stopping one agent changes nothing about the other agent's tokens, rate window, budget or state; only the global switch stops both.

An operator action that clears a kill so calls pass again. It needs an operator name, is written to the audit trail, and never happens by itself for a manual kill. A cap trip is reset the same way, or by auto-reset for rate trips only.
An explicit option: after a cooldown, a rate trip is cleared by the gateway itself and an audited auto_reset entry is written. The cooldown here is an invented demo number.

Kill and unrevoke are state-changing requests, so a page on another origin must not be able to send them. The server refuses a cross-origin request with 403, requires JSON bodies and a loopback Host. Tests prove a cross-origin page cannot kill or unrevoke.

An append-only record of every trip, kill, unrevoke, auto-reset and reset. Each entry carries an HMAC hash of its content and the previous entry's hash, so changing or removing an entry breaks the chain. It lives in memory and is lost when the process exits.
Any string an agent or operator supplies is redacted and shown as plain text: hidden and control characters are made visible and sizes are bounded, so it cannot act as markup or instructions.

Everything is a mock: a scripted agent, a mock gateway and a stub token service on loopback. There is no tenant and no real model. How real PingOne products implement revoke and caps is as modelled in the demo environment, UNVERIFIED against product documentation; the app makes no claim about real product defaults, limits or latency.

A registered identity for a workload (a Kubernetes service account, a CI job and so on) whose agents authenticate with the short-lived token their own platform issues, so nothing long-lived is stored in the workload. Federated Identity is the display name from the H2 2026 deck; the Privilege API object is still called NonHumanIdentity. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

The short-lived token a workload's own platform mints and rotates for it. The platform does not know about a revoke in Privilege, so after a revoke it keeps issuing valid tokens that the gateway refuses. In this lab it is a real RS256 token in Live mode, signed with a throwaway key made in the process, and a fixed marker in Mock mode.

The gateway matches issuer and subject exactly, the audience is mandatory, and expiry is required with a capped lifetime (the deck says default one hour). Only asymmetric signature algorithms are accepted. Per the deck, Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

One operator action after which the gateway refuses the workload on its next request, on every service family (MCP, A2A, LLM) and on an agent access key that names the identity, even though the platform token still validates. The deck says the workload is cut off immediately and gives no number; this lab counts requests, not milliseconds. What a real revoke does to the record, in flight requests or backend credentials is not stated in the deck. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

term: Key set refresh and last known good
definition: The gateway holds the issuer's published key set, refreshes it every fifteen minutes and keeps the last known good set through an issuer outage (per the deck). In this lab an outage does not bring a revoked identity back, and a not-revoked identity keeps working on the cached set. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Every claim in the Federated Identity section is tagged with where it comes from: deck claim, console swagger name (schema only), lab reading, lab-invented, measured (our note) or roadmap. A swagger name proves a field exists, not how it behaves. Ping's numbers are never presented as this lab's.
